summary: Describes the architecture of Internet email, which has grown in scale and complexity over decades while evolving rather than being replaced. It gives a common vocabulary for the components and roles involved, so people can discuss the system consistently. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Internet mail passes through several services before a recipient reads a message. RFC 5598 names the people and systems involved and explains their roles. It provides a common model for discussing email rather than defining a new protocol.

subtitle: A shared map of Internet mail's roles, message identities, and transfer components.

tldr.problem: Internet mail grew into a complex service with many independent operators and components. Different groups used different models and meanings for the same terms.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the architecture through its actors, identities, and functions, including users, the Message Handling Service, administrative domains, MUAs, MSAs, MTAs, MDAs, and message stores.
tldr.outcome: The document provides a shared vocabulary and model for discussion. It introduces no new protocol or requirements.

today: RFC 5598 is Informational and describes the Internet mail architecture as it stood at publication. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Mail Needs a Common Model
sections.content:
Internet mail evolved over decades while preserving much of its existing service. SMTP transfers messages, Internet Mail Format describes the message object, and MIME supports multimedia content.

The system involves independent operators and many components. RFC 5598 describes the existing architecture after the fact so people can use shared terms when discussing technical, operational, and policy questions.
sections.plainLanguage: Email developed through many separate systems and gradual changes. This RFC gives those systems and their relationships common names.

sections.title: Users, Mail Services, and Administrators
sections.content:
The RFC groups actors into Users, the Message Handling Service (MHS), and Administrative Management Domains (ADMDs). User roles include Authors, Recipients, Return Handlers, and Mediators. A Mediator receives and reposts messages, as a mailing list does.

MHS roles include an Originator that accepts a message for posting, Relays that store and forward it, Gateways that connect different mail services, and a Receiver that handles final delivery. An ADMD is a group of services under one administrative authority.
sections.plainLanguage: Authors create messages, recipients read them, and mail services transfer them. Administrative domains mark where one operator's policies and responsibilities meet another's.

sections.title: Addresses and Message Identifiers
sections.content:
A mailbox address has a local part and a domain name separated by an at-sign. The domain is interpreted globally; the local part is interpreted by the domain named on the right.

A Message-ID identifies message content, while an ENVID identifies one transit through the MHS. The SMTP MailFrom address identifies where transfer notices go; it is not necessarily the message's Author. These identifiers belong to different parts of the service and are set by different actors.
sections.plainLanguage: An email address combines a locally interpreted name with a domain. A Message-ID identifies content, while an ENVID labels a transfer and MailFrom receives transfer notices.

sections.title: How a Message Moves Through the System
sections.content:
The architecture describes six basic functions: the Message, Message User Agent (MUA), Message Submission Agent (MSA), Message Transfer Agent (MTA), Message Delivery Agent (MDA), and Message Store (MS). The Author's MUA submits a message to an MSA, which applies local policy and passes it into the transfer service.

MTAs relay and store the message until an MDA delivers it to the recipient's environment. The recipient's MUA reads from a message store, often using POP or IMAP. A single implementation can combine several of these functions.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender's mail program submits a message, relays move it between systems, and a delivery agent places it where the recipient can read it. One program or server can perform more than one role.

sections.title: Mediators, Security, and International Mail
sections.content:
Mediators create a new posting based on a message they received. Aliases change an envelope recipient, ReSenders redirect a message while retaining its original author information, mailing lists distribute messages to subscribers, and Gateways translate between different mail services.

The architecture does not require authentication or prevent disclosure; separate specifications provide security mechanisms. The RFC also describes how MIME and related extensions support character sets beyond the original 7-bit US-ASCII basis, including UTF-8 in existing mail.
sections.plainLanguage: A mailing list or gateway acts as a sender when it reposts or transforms a message. Security protections and support for international characters come from other specifications.
